title: Three Indians Rescued From Attacked Black Sea Ship Fly Home From Romania
excerpt: Sahil Sandhu, Ashwini Kumar and Harman Singh — the three Indian seafarers rescued from the attacked MV Royad Mammadov — departed Romania for India on Saturday after a week-long consular operation.
body:
• Sahil Sandhu, Ashwini Kumar and Harman Singh — the three Indian seafarers rescued from the attacked MV Royad Mammadov in the Black Sea — departed Romania for India on Saturday, the Embassy of India in Bucharest announced.
  • Monday's attack on the commercial vessel killed two foreign crew members and injured the three Indians; Romanian authorities led the rescue operation.
  • The Indian mission arranged mobile phones, Indian food, hospital care and coordination with police and doctors, thanking Romanian authorities, Constanta County Hospital and rescue teams.
  • India condemned the attack and reiterated its call for dialogue and diplomacy; it also highlighted its seat in a 25-nation UN group on the safety of shipping and seafarers.

Three Indian nationals rescued from the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov, which came under attack in the Black Sea on Monday, have departed Romania for India, the Embassy of India in Bucharest said on Saturday. The departure closes a week-long consular operation that began with the rescue of the injured crew.

"Three Indian nationals, Shri Sahil Sandhu, Shri Ashwini Kumar, and Shri Harman Singh, departed for India today. The Embassy provided all necessary support and assistance to facilitate their return," the mission posted on X.

From rescue to repatriation

The three seafarers were pulled to safety on Tuesday after the attack, in which two foreign crew members were killed. An embassy representative visited them on Wednesday: two were accommodated at a hotel while the third was undergoing treatment at Constanta County Hospital. All three were reported in stable condition.

https://x.com/NewsArenaIndia/status/2109139421992018217

Essential items, including mobile phones, were facilitated through the shipping company's local agent, while Indian food was arranged through a local Indian restaurant. The embassy representative also met local police authorities, the shipping company's agent and the treating medical doctors to coordinate further assistance.

"We express our sincere gratitude to the Romanian authorities, Constanta County Hospital, and the Romanian rescue teams for their invaluable assistance, cooperation and support," the embassy said.

New Delhi's response

The Ministry of External Affairs condemned the attack and said attacks targeting commercial vessels threaten commercial shipping and endanger the lives of the seafaring community. "The targeting of traffic in international waterways is severely undermining global commerce and the welfare of people across the world," the ministry said, reiterating India's call for dialogue and diplomacy to bring an end to ongoing conflicts.

"The targeting of traffic in international waterways is severely undermining global commerce and the welfare of people across the world. We continue to call for dialogue and diplomacy to bring an end to the ongoing conflicts."

— Ministry of External Affairs, India

India also highlighted its role in the 25-nation Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, launched jointly with Liberia during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, to promote the safety of merchant crews and commercial shipping against targeted attacks.

Diaspora angle

India is one of the world's largest suppliers of seafarers — Indian crews account for roughly one in ten sailors on the world's merchant ships — so attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea strike directly at Indian families whose breadwinners work these routes. New Delhi's rapid repatriation operation underscores how central seafarer safety has become to its foreign policy.

What's next

India has noted a string of attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea over the last few days, and shipping companies and insurers will be reassessing routes and risk premiums. For the thousands of Indian seafarers working in conflict-adjacent waters, the question is whether the corridor stays navigable — or becomes too dangerous to transit at any price.
